drills.q: A Service has healthy endpoints and kubectl port-forward to the backing pod works, but connecting to the ClusterIP times out. What are the two separate failure domains to check, in order?
drills.a: First isolate: does raw pod-to-pod connectivity work at all (bypass the Service, hit the pod IP directly) — if not, it's a CNI/routing problem. If direct pod IP works but the Service VIP doesn't, check kube-proxy's actual programmed state for its mode (iptables rules / ipvsadm / eBPF debug tool) and check NetworkPolicy separately, since these are three genuinely distinct layers.

drills.q: Security audit finds that pods with an 'ingress-restricted' NetworkPolicy can still reach any external endpoint outbound. Explain the mechanism, not just 'they forgot egress.'
drills.a: NetworkPolicy is direction-specific and additive. A policy selecting those pods only for Ingress flips ingress to default-deny-then-allow, but egress was never selected by any policy, so it remains at its original default-allow posture — nothing in the ingress policy touches egress at all, by design, not as a side effect that could have been anticipated from the ingress rule alone.

drills.q: A cluster running plain Flannel has a full set of well-written NetworkPolicy objects covering every namespace. Is the cluster actually protected? How would you verify?
drills.a: Not necessarily — NetworkPolicy is only enforced if the CNI implements a policy controller; plain Flannel implements none by default, so the objects can be fully valid and stored while having zero effect on traffic. Verify by direct testing: deploy two pods, apply a deny policy between them, and actually attempt the traffic that should now be blocked — if it still succeeds, enforcement isn't happening regardless of how correct the YAML looks.

drills.q: A service makes its first call to a new external API and it's consistently ~4x slower than subsequent calls to the same host. What's the mechanism and the fix?
drills.a: ndots:5 default: the hostname (fewer than 5 dots) gets every in-cluster search suffix tried first, each a real round trip returning a negative response, before the correct absolute lookup finally succeeds on the last attempt. Subsequent calls are fast because the successful (and often the negative) results get cached. Fix: trailing-dot the hostname in code to fully-qualify it, or tune ndots via pod.spec.dnsConfig, or deploy NodeLocal DNSCache.

drills.q: Your team is planning a new cluster in August 2026 and debating Ingress vs Gateway API. What's the actual current guidance, and does ingress-nginx's retirement change the calculus?
drills.a: Gateway API's core resources are GA and production-ready with a better role-oriented model (infra owns Gateway, app teams own HTTPRoute) and native traffic splitting Ingress can't do portably. The core Ingress API itself isn't going away (SIG-Network says maintained indefinitely) — but ingress-nginx specifically is retiring (best-effort only through March 2026, then archived), which is a forcing function only for teams using that specific controller. For a brand new cluster, Gateway API is the reasonable default choice today; TCPRoute/UDPRoute are still experimental so non-HTTP protocol needs may still need Ingress or a controller-specific solution.

drills.q: Why does kube-proxy still default to iptables mode given IPVS and nftables both outperform it, and IPVS is now deprecated?
drills.a: iptables remains default purely for backward compatibility across the huge existing installed base — the project has been explicit about this. IPVS (O(1) hash lookup, fixed iptables's O(n) chain-walk problem) is deprecated as of 1.35. nftables (stable since 1.33, atomic rule replacement) is the intended long-term replacement, but changing a core networking dataplane's default carries real upgrade risk at Kubernetes's installed-base scale, so it hasn't been made default yet with no committed timeline.

drills.q: Pods on node A can reach pods on node B for small requests but larger payloads silently fail or hang. What's a likely CNI-level cause and why?
drills.a: MTU mismatch — VXLAN-style overlay encapsulation (common in Flannel and similar overlay CNIs) adds header overhead that an unadjusted node/interface MTU doesn't account for, causing silent drops for packets that exceed the effective MTU once encapsulation overhead is added. Check CNI daemon logs and verify the node interface MTU is set several dozen bytes below the physical MTU to leave room for encapsulation.

drills.q: Why does a headless Service need to exist for a StatefulSet, and what specifically would a normal ClusterIP Service fail to provide?
drills.a: A normal ClusterIP Service returns one A record for a virtual IP, load-balancing across whichever pod happens to answer — it has no concept of addressing a specific ordinal. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns individual pod IPs directly (and per-pod names via the StatefulSet's serviceName), giving each replica an individually resolvable DNS identity, which is exactly what's needed to reach 'the primary at ordinal 0' specifically rather than any interchangeable pod.
